boundary: C reductions that drive the real upstream function, compiled verbatim from the 17.5 pin, with no server in the process
title: Memory-safety defects in PostgreSQL 17.5 reduced to C against the real upstream function
note: The counterpart to sql-repros and mmgr-repros, and the reason it exists: both of those are palloc clients, so every defect in them is nested by construction. PostgreSQL's client side is not -- libpq, psql, pg_dump and fe_utils call malloc, realloc and free directly, about 990 call sites against the backend's 82 -- so a defect here is a libc client and is non-nested. Without this corpus the study has no non-nested arm to compare against, and a mechanism's silence on a nested defect cannot be attributed to the nesting. These cases are C reductions, not SQL: the defect is in the client process and no statement sent to a server can reach it. Each drives the real upstream function with a constructed input, the way mmgr-repros drives the real aset and slab. That also makes them freestanding domains, so unlike sql-repros they need no application VM. All five were reproduced on the host under ASan on 2026-10-06 against shared/corpus.h and shared/driver.c, each driving the real upstream function copied verbatim from the pin (shared/upstream_libpq.c, upstream_pgdump.c, upstream_ecpg.c, upstream_saslprep.c, upstream_bbstreamer.c). Each case's host-asan oracle records the faulting access, its size and the exact size of the region it ran off, so the reduction is checkable against the arithmetic in its live_proof rather than taken on trust. RESULT ON THE PURECAP ARM, 2026-10-06: 3 of 5 detected (00, 02, 04 all SIGPROT with their PG_DEFECT marker printed first), 2 reached-silent (01, 03). Every one of the five verdicts is predicted by one measured fact, and the fact is worth more than the ratio: this guest's malloc rounds capability bounds to a SIZE CLASS, not to the request. Measured requested->granted pairs: 1->16, 4->16, 8->16, 16->16, 24->32, 32->32, 100->112, 400->448, 4096->4096. Lining the cases up against it: 00 writes 4096 bytes into an 8-byte request (cap 16) and faults; 02 walks ~4 GiB from a 1-byte request (cap 16) and faults; 04 reads 24 bytes from offset 24 of a 24-byte request (cap 32) and crosses at offset 32, so it faults; 01 reads offset 400 of a 400-byte request (cap 448) and does not; 03 reads offset 4 of a 4-byte request (cap 16) and does not. So a malloc-granular capability machine sees an overrun exactly when it exceeds the ALLOCATOR'S ROUNDING, not when it exceeds the object. Two of five real CVE-class defects are invisible here for that reason alone, with no nesting involved at all -- which is a second blind spot, independent of the one this corpus was built to measure, and it narrows the claim that non-nested defects are the ones such a mechanism catches. On fault attribution: these cases cannot use mmgr-repros' .globl label on the faulting instruction, because in three of the five that instruction is inside a function copied verbatim from upstream and a label would make the copy no longer verbatim. The handler in shared/driver.c reports the faulting PC and the return address as offsets from a function the case names instead, which attributes the fault without touching upstream code; case 00 is why both are reported, since its fault is inside libc's memcpy and only the return address lands in pqGetnchar. One field is NOT usable here and is recorded so nobody relies on it: on this guest SIGPROT arrives with si_addr equal to the faulting PC, not to the data address -- measured as addr==pc on all three faulting cases -- so the fault address cannot be cross-checked against an object's bounds from siginfo. Renamed from c-repros on 2026-10-06, and the old boundary text -- "libpq and the client tools, which allocate from libc and not from a memory context" -- was wrong and is replaced. libpq has a nested allocator of its own: fe-exec.c:563 pqResultAlloc carves every PGresult's subsidiary storage out of 2048-byte PGRESULT_DATA_BLOCKSIZE blocks it mallocs, and upstream's own comment calls it "our trivial space allocator". So a client-side defect is not non-nested by virtue of being client-side. The five cases here are non-nested because of what each one touches -- a caller's buffer, a pg_dump array, an ecpg host variable, an application password, a pg_basebackup chunk -- and not one of them touches PGresult storage. That is a property of the selection, not of the client side, and a future case on PGresult memory would belong here with allocator_layer set accordingly. CORRECTION, 2026-10-06. This corpus previously recorded that the two Capstone arms could not host these cases, on the grounds that a domain's malloc is itself a nested allocator (the spatial arm) or refuses outright (the sublet arm). That was wrong, and it pointed at the wrong code: both of those files, memory-contexts/src/allocators/spatial/backing-allocator.c and .../sublet/unsupported-allocators.c, belong to the memory-contexts replay study and are linked into neither arm image -- checked by symbol, pg_subpool_refuse is absent from both postgres.dom binaries. What an arm image links is ports/musl-capstone/runtime/level0.c, whose CAPSTONE_LEVEL0_OBJECT_BOUNDS has been on by default since 2026-09-30 and which neither arm overrides; malloc there narrows what it returns to the bytes asked for, and the built binaries carry six shrink instructions inside malloc itself. So a non-nested object has always been hostable on both arms. What was missing was a domain build, and shared/build-domain.sh is now it: 5 of 5 cases build against each arm's SDK. Nothing was relaxed to achieve this, and the sublet arm's refusing malloc, whose job is to catch a PostgreSQL memory manager reaching an unadapted libc path, is not part of this build and is unchanged. A prediction worth recording before the run, because it is falsifiable: the purecap guest rounds bounds to a size class and so missed 01 and 03, while level0 bounds the request exactly, so both should be reported here. If they are not, the difference is not bounds granularity and this note is wrong.
